entities.summary: Philotas was an ancient Greek dithyrambic poet and musician, born in Cythera (Creta e Peleponeso, 430–400 BCE), who gained recognition for his victory over his contemporary Timotheus of Miletus (Timotheos of Milou), a renowned Greek poet and musician. Philotas was a disciple of Philoxenus of Cythera, who was said to have taught him the art of the dithyramb. The dithyramb was a traditional form of Greek poetry and music that was used in religious and civic contexts. Philotas' musical talents were so renowned that he was invited to perform at the court of the Macedonian king Philip II (Philippos II of Makedon), who was father of Alexander the Great. Despite his achievements, very little is known about Philotas' life beyond his victory over Timotheus and his association with Philoxenus, which suggests that his cultural and historical impact was largely overshadowed by that of his more famous contemporaries. As a result, he is considered one of the 'minor' figures of ancient Greek poetry and music, yet his legacy remains an important testament to the enduring power of the dithyramb and the rich cultural heritage of ancient Greece.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Philotas was a minor figure in ancient Greek poetry and music, but his victory over Timotheus of Miletus and his association with Philoxenus and the Macedonian royal court helped to promote the cultural and artistic achievements of ancient Greece beyond its borders.
